publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Prevalence of Depression Symptoms in US Adults Before and During the COVID-19 Pandemic

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the prevalence of depression symptoms in US adults during the first fortnight of the COVID-19 pandemic, set against a pre-pandemic national baseline measured with THE SAME INSTRUMENT
span.quote: This nationally representative survey study used 2 population-based surveys of US adults aged 18 or older. During COVID-19, estimates were derived from the COVID-19 and Life Stressors Impact on Mental Health and Well-being study, conducted from March 31, 2020, to April 13, 2020. Before COVID-19 estimates were derived from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, conducted from 2017 to 2018.

span.label: how much higher depression symptom prevalence was during COVID-19 than before it, and which social and economic resources predicted it
span.quote: This survey study found that prevalence of depression symptoms in the US increased more than 3-fold during the COVID-19 pandemic, from 8.5% before COVID-19 to 27.8% during COVID-19.

span.label: the first nationally representative before-and-during comparison of US depression symptoms on a single validated screener, and a severity gradient showing the increase is largest at the severe end
span.quote: Overall, prevalence was 1.5-fold higher for mild depression symptoms, 2.6-fold higher for moderate depression symptoms, 3.7-fold higher for moderately severe depression symptoms, and 7.5-fold higher for severe depression symptoms categories during COVID-19 compared with before COVID-19.

span.label: existence
span.quote: This survey study found that prevalence of depression symptoms in the US increased more than 3-fold during the COVID-19 pandemic, from 8.5% before COVID-19 to 27.8% during COVID-19.

span.label: a population-scale rise in depression symptoms concentrated in the lowest-resource groups, rising monotonically with counted stressor exposure
span.quote: Experiencing more COVID-19 stressors was also associated with greater odds of depression symptoms compared with people with low stressor exposure (medium: OR, 1.77 [95% CI, 1.16-2.71]); high: OR, 3.05 [95% CI, 1.95-4.77]).

span.label: two probability-based population surveys compared cross-sectionally - NHANES 2017-2018 by household interview, and the CLIMB study of the AmeriSpeak online panel from 31 March to 13 April 2020 - both scored with PHQ-9, weighted, then multivariable logistic regression within the during-COVID arm
span.term: two probability-based population surveys compared cross-sectionally - NHANES 2017-2018 by household interview, and the CLIMB study of the AmeriSpeak online panel from 31 March to 13 April 2020 - both scored with PHQ-9, weighted, then multivariable logistic regression within the during-COVID arm
span.quote: This nationally representative survey study used 2 population-based surveys of US adults aged 18 or older. During COVID-19, estimates were derived from the COVID-19 and Life Stressors Impact on Mental Health and Well-being study, conducted from March 31, 2020, to April 13, 2020. Before COVID-19 estimates were derived from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, conducted from 2017 to 2018.

span.label: the explanation offered is material rather than clinical - income, savings under $5000, and a count of realised stressors such as job loss - and each is carried by an odds ratio with an interval rather than by a narrative
span.quote: Compared with individuals with an annual household income of $75 000 or more, those with a household income of $19 999 or less had 2.4-fold increased odds of depression symptoms (OR, 2.37 [95% CI, 1.26-4.43]). Individuals with household savings less than $5000 had 1.5-fold increased odds of depression symptoms (OR, 1.52 [95% CI, 1.02-2.26]).

span.label: the dose-response across the stressor score is the strongest internal evidence for the material reading: low is the reference, medium 1.77 and high 3.05, ordered, and BOTH INTERVALS EXCLUDE 1. They do NOT exclude each other - 1.16-2.71 and 1.95-4.77 overlap - so the ordering of the two raised categories is not established by this quote, only their separation from the reference
span.quote: Experiencing more COVID-19 stressors was also associated with greater odds of depression symptoms compared with people with low stressor exposure (medium: OR, 1.77 [95% CI, 1.16-2.71]); high: OR, 3.05 [95% CI, 1.95-4.77]).

span.label: THE TWO ARMS ARE TWO DIFFERENT SURVEYS OF DIFFERENT PEOPLE, and the paper says so first: `we are assessing different individuals ... the NHANES data can provide only a PROXY for the true baseline`. The instrument is held constant and the sampling frame is not
span.quote: First, we compare 2 cross-sectional data sources; by comparing NHANES and CLIMB, we are assessing different individuals. We do not survey the same individuals over time, so the NHANES data can provide only a proxy for the true baseline level of depression for CLIMB participants. Differences in prevalence of depression between groups may in part be driven by differences in demographic characteristics, random selection, recruitment, and sampling frame.

span.label: the during-COVID arm is conditioned on things the baseline arm is not: respondents had to SPEAK ENGLISH and to have COMPLETED AN AMERISPEAK SURVEY IN THE PREVIOUS SIX MONTHS, and 94.2% answered over the internet. NHANES imposes none of these
span.quote: Adults aged 18 years or older who could speak English and who had completed an AmeriSpeak survey in the past 6 months were eligible to take the survey. In total, 1470 participants completed the survey, representing a survey completion rate of 64.3% of sampled panelists. The survey was conducted mainly over the internet (1385 participants [94.2%]) with a small number conducted over the telephone (85 participants [5.8%]).

span.label: and the panel was PAID - a cash equivalent of $3 - which NHANES participants are not. The paper reports the payment in the methods and does not carry it into the limitations
span.quote: As members of the AmeriSpeak panel, participants are invited to participate in several surveys per month and were paid a cash equivalent of $3 for completing this survey.

span.label: the panel also came in with MORE PRIOR DEPRESSION than the national baseline, 18.8% against 16.5%. The paper reports the gap, calls it small, and then states plainly that `IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO ANTICIPATE HOW THE DIFFERENCE ... COULD, IF AT ALL, AFFECT THE MAGNITUDE` - an unresolved confound, declared as unresolved
span.quote: Second, some differences in the NHANES and CLIMB depression estimates may be owing to the differences in baseline mental health across participants; for example, estimates of responses to the assessment of previous diagnosis of depression from 2016 suggest that participants in the AmeriSpeak panel had a 2.3–percentage point higher prevalence of previous diagnosis of depression than the national baseline as measured through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (18.8% in AmeriSpeak vs 16.5% in the national baseline).

span.label: the comparability argument is an ARGUMENT, not a demonstration: both frames are probability-based and address-based, therefore `mitigating this concern`. No empirical check that the two frames yield the same PHQ-9 distribution on a common population is offered, and none could be from these data
span.quote: However, these are both population-representative surveys, drawn randomly with probability-based sampling using address-based sampling of US households, mitigating this concern.

span.label: the instrument is a SCREENER and the paper is the one in this group that says so: `a diagnosis of depression is ultimately a diagnosis made by a clinician`. 27.8% is 27.8% scoring at or above 10 on the PHQ-9
span.quote: Fourth, we are using a well-established and validated depression screener. While this provides probably the best possible assessment of population-level burden of depression, a diagnosis of depression is ultimately a diagnosis made by a clinician.

span.label: the instrument is held identical across the two arms, and identity of measurement is named as the thing that makes the comparison possible
span.note: eliminates: instrument change as the explanation of the before-during difference - the one confound qiu2020 and gao2020 cannot exclude against each other · outcome: held
span.quote: We used identical measures of outcome assessment to enable cross-study comparability.

span.label: whether the two samples are drawn from comparable frames
span.note: eliminates: nothing empirically - both frames are probability-based and address-based, which is offered as `mitigating this concern`, but the arms are DIFFERENT INDIVIDUALS and the baseline is called a PROXY by the authors · outcome: partial
span.quote: However, these are both population-representative surveys, drawn randomly with probability-based sampling using address-based sampling of US households, mitigating this concern.

span.label: whether the panel arm was already more depressed than the population before COVID-19
span.note: eliminates: nothing - measured at 18.8% prior diagnosis against a national 16.5%, and the authors state it is IMPOSSIBLE TO ANTICIPATE how that difference bears on the result · outcome: failed
span.quote: Second, some differences in the NHANES and CLIMB depression estimates may be owing to the differences in baseline mental health across participants; for example, estimates of responses to the assessment of previous diagnosis of depression from 2016 suggest that participants in the AmeriSpeak panel had a 2.3–percentage point higher prevalence of previous diagnosis of depression than the national baseline as measured through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (18.8% in AmeriSpeak vs 16.5% in the national baseline).

span.label: the multivariable model controls sex, age, race/ethnicity, household size, education, marital status, income, savings and stressor score simultaneously
span.note: eliminates: demography as the explanation of the income, savings and stressor gradients - all three survive adjustment with intervals excluding 1 · outcome: held
span.quote: Among the CLIMB sample, after controlling for sex, age, race/ethnicity, household size, education, marital status, household income, household savings, and COVID-19 stressor score, participants with lower social and economic resources and with higher COVID-19 stressor scores had higher odds of depression symptoms compared with participants with higher social and economic resources or lower COVID-19 stressor scores

span.label: Patient Health Questionnaire–9
span.quote: Depression symptoms in both studies were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire–9, a clinically validated survey with a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 88% at a cutoff score of 10 or higher.

span.label: sensitivity
span.quote: Depression symptoms in both studies were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire–9, a clinically validated survey with a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 88% at a cutoff score of 10 or higher.

span.label: specificity
span.quote: Depression symptoms in both studies were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire–9, a clinically validated survey with a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 88% at a cutoff score of 10 or higher.

span.label: depression symptoms
span.quote: This survey study found that prevalence of depression symptoms in the US increased more than 3-fold during the COVID-19 pandemic, from 8.5% before COVID-19 to 27.8% during COVID-19.

span.label: major depressive disorder
span.quote: Our estimates of pre–COVID-19 depressive symptoms are consistent with other population-level nationally representative studies that captured different constructs of depression; in 2018, 4.7% of adults aged 18 years or older surveyed in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health had major depressive disorder with severe impairment, compared with 8.5% of adults in the NHANES having depression symptoms.

span.label: COVID-19 stressors
span.quote: We assessed 13 stressors based on prior studies conducted after traumatic events. 20 , 21 Examples of COVID-19 stressors included losing a job, death of someone close to you owing to COVID-19, and having financial problems. We excluded stressors that were capturing constructs applicable only to specific groups and created a score ranging from 0 to 13 to measure cumulative exposure to COVID-19 stressors. We divided the scores into thirds to measure low, medium, and high exposure to COVID-19-induced stressors. Cutoffs for stressor score categories were low (score, 0-2), medium (score, 3-4), and high (score, 5-13).

span.label: stressor score
span.quote: We assessed 13 stressors based on prior studies conducted after traumatic events. 20 , 21 Examples of COVID-19 stressors included losing a job, death of someone close to you owing to COVID-19, and having financial problems. We excluded stressors that were capturing constructs applicable only to specific groups and created a score ranging from 0 to 13 to measure cumulative exposure to COVID-19 stressors. We divided the scores into thirds to measure low, medium, and high exposure to COVID-19-induced stressors. Cutoffs for stressor score categories were low (score, 0-2), medium (score, 3-4), and high (score, 5-13).

span.label: screener
span.quote: Fourth, we are using a well-established and validated depression screener. While this provides probably the best possible assessment of population-level burden of depression, a diagnosis of depression is ultimately a diagnosis made by a clinician.

span.label: depression symptoms - AS OPERATIONALISED HERE, A PHQ-9 SCORE OF 10 OR GREATER, on an instrument validated BEFORE the study with a published sensitivity of 88% and specificity of 88% AT THAT CUT-OFF. The threshold is inherited, not asserted, and that is the single largest methodological difference between this paper and qiu2020
span.quote: Depression symptoms in both studies were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire–9, a clinically validated survey with a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 88% at a cutoff score of 10 or higher.

span.label: the severity categories - none 0-4, mild 5-9, moderate 10-14, moderately severe 15-19, severe >=20, CITED TO THE VALIDATION PAPER rather than chosen here. The flattened `19` after the list is that citation marker
span.quote: Depression symptom categories were defined as none (score, 0-4), mild (score, 5-9), moderate (score, 10-14), moderately severe (score, 15-19), and severe (score, ≥20). Binary classification of depression symptoms was defined by a score of 10 or greater.

span.label: COVID-19 stressor exposure - A COUNT, 0 to 13, OF REALISED EVENTS (job loss, a death, financial problems), then CUT INTO THIRDS. AND THE THIRDS ARE NOT THIRDS OF THE SCALE: equal parts of 0-13 would break at about 4 and 9, and the paper breaks at 2 and 4. The cut points are therefore fitted to the RESPONSES, not to the instrument, so `high exposure` means `in the upper part of THIS survey` and does not transfer
span.quote: We assessed 13 stressors based on prior studies conducted after traumatic events. 20 , 21 Examples of COVID-19 stressors included losing a job, death of someone close to you owing to COVID-19, and having financial problems. We excluded stressors that were capturing constructs applicable only to specific groups and created a score ranging from 0 to 13 to measure cumulative exposure to COVID-19 stressors. We divided the scores into thirds to measure low, medium, and high exposure to COVID-19-induced stressors. Cutoffs for stressor score categories were low (score, 0-2), medium (score, 3-4), and high (score, 5-13).

span.label: `consistent` - USED HERE FOR TWO NUMBERS THAT DIFFER BY NEARLY A FACTOR OF TWO. 4.7% with major depressive disorder with severe impairment against 8.5% with depression symptoms, same country, adjacent years, and the paper calls the pair consistent BECAUSE IT NAMES THE CONSTRUCT DIFFERENCE. This is the correct use of the word and it is rare
span.quote: Our estimates of pre–COVID-19 depressive symptoms are consistent with other population-level nationally representative studies that captured different constructs of depression; in 2018, 4.7% of adults aged 18 years or older surveyed in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health had major depressive disorder with severe impairment, compared with 8.5% of adults in the NHANES having depression symptoms.

span.label: major depressive disorder - NOT MEASURED HERE and explicitly `a MORE SEVERE measure of depression` than this paper's outcome. The paper uses the ordering to make a PREDICTION - that MDD estimates should rise too - rather than to claim it found MDD
span.quote: While major depressive disorder is a more severe measure of depression, based on the results of our study, we may expect to see increases in the presence of major depressive disorder in other studies conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic.

span.quote: What is the burden of depression symptoms among US adults during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic compared with before COVID-19, and what are the risk factors associated with depression symptoms? Findings In this survey study that included 1441 respondents from during the COVID-19 pandemic and 5065 respondents from before the pandemic, depression symptom prevalence was more than 3-fold higher during the COVID-19 pandemic than before.

span.label: supports → the 2014 review finding that depression increases during and after traumatic events - the paper says in its own words that it ADDS TO this literature
span.quote: Findings from a 2014 review 3 on trauma and mental health suggest that depression increases during and after traumatic events; our study adds to this literature.

span.label: extends → Ni et al's before-and-after study of the 2019 Hong Kong protests, WHICH USED THE SAME INSTRUMENT - the paper makes instrument identity the explicit licence for comparing its numbers with theirs
span.quote: A 2020 study by Ni et al 8 analyzed depression symptoms before and after political unrest in Hong Kong using the same measure of depression symptoms we deployed in this study. They reported national depression symptoms prevalence before the unrest to be 6.5% (compared with 8.5% in our pre–COVID-19 US sample) and 11.2% in 2019 during unrest (compared with 27.8% in our during–COVID-19 sample).

span.label: supports → Lai et al's finding of substantial depression among Chinese health care workers - offered as consistent WHILE naming the population and timing differences that stop the percentages being read against each other
span.quote: In a study of health care workers in Hubei province and surrounding regions, Lai et al 15 found similar levels of depression: 49.6% of participants had no depression (vs 47.5% of participants in the CLIMB sample), while 35.6% of participants had mild depression (vs 24.6% in the CLIMB sample), 8.6% of participants had moderate depression (vs 14.8% in the CLIMB sample), and 6.2% of participants had moderately severe depression (vs 7.9% in the CLIMB sample). The Lai et al 15 sample in China included only health care professionals and was concentrated in the Hubei region, while our sample included a representative sample of all US residents and sampled the whole country.

span.quote: Depression symptoms in both studies were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire–9, a clinically validated survey with a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 88% at a cutoff score of 10 or higher.

span.quote: Our estimates of pre–COVID-19 depressive symptoms are consistent with other population-level nationally representative studies that captured different constructs of depression; in 2018, 4.7% of adults aged 18 years or older surveyed in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health had major depressive disorder with severe impairment, compared with 8.5% of adults in the NHANES having depression symptoms.

span.label: OR
span.quote: Experiencing more COVID-19 stressors was also associated with greater odds of depression symptoms compared with people with low stressor exposure (medium: OR, 1.77 [95% CI, 1.16-2.71]); high: OR, 3.05 [95% CI, 1.95-4.77]).

span.label: 95% CI
span.quote: Experiencing more COVID-19 stressors was also associated with greater odds of depression symptoms compared with people with low stressor exposure (medium: OR, 1.77 [95% CI, 1.16-2.71]); high: OR, 3.05 [95% CI, 1.95-4.77]).

span.label: sensitivity
span.quote: Depression symptoms in both studies were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire–9, a clinically validated survey with a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 88% at a cutoff score of 10 or higher.

span.label: household savings
span.quote: Compared with individuals with an annual household income of $75 000 or more, those with a household income of $19 999 or less had 2.4-fold increased odds of depression symptoms (OR, 2.37 [95% CI, 1.26-4.43]). Individuals with household savings less than $5000 had 1.5-fold increased odds of depression symptoms (OR, 1.52 [95% CI, 1.02-2.26]).
